title: Blue sunsets on Mars
hook: On Mars the dusty daytime sky looks butterscotch and the sunset glows blue.
peek: Earth has blue days and red sunsets. Mars does the opposite. Its dusty daytime sky looks tan or pinkish, but as the Sun goes down a cool blue glow gathers around it, as NASA's rovers have photographed many times.
lede: On Earth, air molecules scatter blue light all over the sky by day, and sunsets turn red. Mars swaps the colours. Its air is thin, about 1% as dense as ours, and full of fine dust, which gives the daytime sky a butterscotch tint. At sunset, though, a pale blue halo forms around the Sun, captured by the Pathfinder, Spirit and Curiosity cameras.

bullets.text: The dust grains are very fine, around a micrometre across. Grains that size send blue light onward in roughly the direction it was already travelling, so the blue stays close to the Sun rather than spreading across the sky.

bullets.opening: Why the blue shows at sunset
bullets.text: Near the horizon, sunlight crosses far more dusty air on its way to the camera. That long path strengthens the forward-scattered blue around the Sun while the rest of the sky darkens.
In April 2015, NASA's Curiosity rover photographed a sunset over Gale Crater. The colours were calibrated to approximate what a person's eyes would see: a bluish glow around a small, pale Sun.
Mars is about one and a half times farther from the Sun than Earth, so the setting Sun looks only about two thirds as wide as it does from home.
